items.text: Major earthquake (USGS event us6000tjl2). Asocapitales published a situation report on impacts across Colombian capital cities.
Quake with epicenter near Los Santos, Santander (SGC), felt in Bucaramanga.
Bucaramanga stepped up building prevention measures (Vanguardia); UIS is planning a seismic-risk diagnosis for the city (Caracol).

blocks.html: No damage reports found for Bucaramanga towers in the sources reviewed. That is an absence of reports, not a confirmation that every building was inspected.

items.title: Post-quake inspection colors
items.html:
The national government unified the methodology for assessing buildings after the quake (UNGRD, Circular 73). Buildings are tagged:
  • Green — safe to occupy
  • Yellow — restricted use / needs further evaluation
  • Red — unsafe, do not occupy

items.title: NSR-10
items.html: Colombia's seismic-resistant building code (Reglamento Colombiano de Construcción Sismo Resistente, 2010). Bucaramanga is in a high seismic-hazard zone, which is why the shortlist rule is towers built 2010 or later. Buildings licensed right around 2010 (e.g. Torre Picasso) are borderline — the license date matters more than the delivery date.

items.title: Law 1796 of 2016 (“Vivienda Segura”)
items.html: Added independent review of structural designs, technical supervision during construction and a technical occupancy certificate for new buildings — a further plus for post-2016-licensed towers.

blocks.title: Renter checklist
items: Ask the administración for the building's construction license (licencia de construcción) number and date — confirms NSR-10 era.
Ask whether the building was inspected after the Aug 2026 quakes and what color it got (green/yellow/red).
Walk the common areas: look for new diagonal cracks in walls, columns, stairwells, and at the parking levels.
Check that elevators were inspected/certified and that the building has a posted evacuation plan and meeting point.
Prefer lower floors or houses/low-rise if unsure; know the stair route from your unit.
Ask whether the copropiedad has earthquake coverage on its common-area insurance policy; consider contents/renter insurance.
Keep a small go-bag (water, documents, flashlight, meds) and register with the US Embassy STEP program.

sections.title: Cost of living & renting as a foreigner

items.title: Co-signer (codeudor)
items.html: Traditional unfurnished leases through an inmobiliaria usually require a Colombian codeudor (co-signer, often with property in Colombia) or a lease-insurance policy (póliza / afianzadora). Foreigners without local credit history often can't meet this — furnished rentals and Airbnb-style monthly stays usually skip it.

items.title: Deposit
items.html: Expect to be asked for a deposit, especially on furnished units (commonly one month — confirm). Get the amount, conditions for return, and an inventory (inventario) of the furniture in writing.

items.title: Contract length
items.html: Standard leases are 12 months. Furnished / temporary rentals are more flexible (monthly), but cost more — compare the Cañaveral furnished vs. unfurnished ranges.

items.title: Visa / length of stay
items.html: US citizens typically enter as visitors for 90 days, extendable to 180 days per calendar year. A longer stay needs a visa (e.g. digital-nomad, pensioner or rentista) — check Migración Colombia / Cancillería before committing to a 12-month lease.
